Chapter 6: The Weight of Memory—Bearing Witness and the Burden of Survival.
Time keeps moving forward, doesn’t it? But for anyone who’s lived through upheaval, the past isn’t so quick to let go. On the reservation, memories hang in the air—sometimes like a warm blanket, other times like a shadow you just can’t shake.
For the man who once saw visions as a boy, life after Wounded Knee brings a whole new kind of struggle. The battles aren’t about weapons anymore. Now, it’s all about memory. It’s about holding onto the truth, even when the world seems eager to forget.
He’s often asked to share his story—to talk about what he’s seen and survived. Maybe it’s a child, looking up with big, curious eyes, wanting to hear about the old days. Or maybe it’s a visitor, someone from far away, notebook ready, hoping to capture stories before they disappear. Every time, he feels that weight—the responsibility to be honest. Because telling the truth means reliving the pain, risking misunderstanding, and opening up wounds that never really healed.
There are days when he just wants to stay quiet, to let the past rest. But he knows, deep down, that silence is its own kind of loss. These stories aren’t just his. They belong to the people, to the land, and to every generation still to come. So he chooses his words with care—words that honor not only the suffering, but also the strength. He talks about the vision that shaped his life, the ceremonies that brought a sense of healing, and the friends and family who never made it this far.
And sometimes, as he speaks, he notices the faces in front of him change. There’s sorrow, of course. But there’s also this spark—a kind of awakening. It’s that moment when someone realizes history isn’t just something buried in the past. It’s alive, right here, shaping the present.
The old man knows that memory is both a burden and a gift. Sure, it can feel heavy. But it can also light the way forward.
Later, when the world grows quiet, he sits alone with his thoughts. He remembers the laughter of children, songs drifting up to the stars, and that deep sense of belonging that once felt unbreakable. Yes, so much has been lost. But he also sees what still endures: the resilience of his people, the power of tradition, and a hope that refuses to fade.
It becomes clear—bearing witness isn’t just about telling stories. It’s about keeping the spirit of the people alive. His memories are more than just his own. They’re threads woven into a much larger tapestry, connecting the past to the present, sorrow to hope. And by sharing them, he makes sure the lessons of his life will live on.
